title: Sources & Sinks
blurb: Secure review starts with two questions: where does attacker-controlled data get IN (a source), and where could bad data do HARM (a sink)? A flaw is untrusted data reaching a sink unchecked. Sort each line. The legend defines the terms.

glossary.Untrusted source: Where attacker-controlled data enters your code — the request query, form, body, headers or route, uploaded files, external API responses. Treat all of it as hostile until proven safe.
glossary.Dangerous sink: An operation that can be abused if fed bad data — running SQL, starting a process, opening a file by path, writing to the HTML response, or deserializing (rebuilding an object from raw text). A flaw is untrusted data reaching one of these unchecked.
glossary.Safe / neither: Code that neither takes in attacker data nor does anything dangerous with it — a constant, a log line, ordinary arithmetic.

levels.title: L1 · In, out, or neither?
levels.prompt: Sort each line: does it bring attacker data IN (source), DO something dangerous (sink), or neither?
levels.hint: Ask two things per line: could an attacker control this value? and could a bad value here cause harm?
levels.explain: Request.Query and Request.Form bring in attacker-controlled data — sources. ExecuteSqlRaw and Process.Start act on data in dangerous ways — sinks. Adding two local ints touches no untrusted input and does nothing risky — safe.

failStates.title: Starting a process is a sink
failStates.explain: Launching an OS process is one of the most dangerous sinks there is — if any part of the command comes from user input, that's command injection (an attacker runs their own commands on your server).

failStates.title: Request.Query is attacker-controlled
failStates.explain: Anything from the request — query, form, headers, body — is a source: the attacker picks the value. It's safe only after you validate it.

levels.title: L2 · More lines to triage
levels.prompt: Same call: source, sink, or neither?
levels.hint: A sink doesn't have to touch a database — files, the HTTP response, and deserialization are sinks too.

items.label: await Response.WriteAsync(userText);
items.note: writes to the HTTP response body

items.label: JsonSerializer.Deserialize<Order>(body);
items.note: rebuilds an object from raw text

levels.explain: Request.Headers is a source (attacker-controlled). Opening a file by path (path could be tainted), writing user text into the response (XSS — the browser could run it as script), and deserializing untrusted text into an object are all sinks. A fixed log line is safe.

failStates.title: Writing user text to the response is a sink
failStates.explain: If you write attacker text straight into the HTML response, the browser may execute it as script — that's cross-site scripting (XSS). Output must be encoded; Razor does this for you, raw Response.WriteAsync does not.

failStates.title: Headers are attacker-controlled too
failStates.explain: Request headers are just as attacker-controlled as the query string — a source. Don't trust them (including things like Host or X-Forwarded-For).
